records.source: אִם־בַּמַּחְתֶּ֛רֶת יִמָּצֵ֥א הַגַּנָּ֖ב וְהֻכָּ֣ה וָמֵ֑ת אֵ֥ין ל֖וֹ דָּמִֽים׃
records.gloss: If in the breaking in is found the thief, and he is struck and dies, there [is] no blood for him.
pieces: Suppose a thief is caught in the act of breaking in, and someone strikes him and he dies. Then there is no bloodguilt for his death.

L.1: If the thief is found in the breaking in, and he is struck and dies, [there is] no blood[guilt] for him.

R.1: Someone might catch a thief breaking in at night and strike him so hard that he dies. If that happens, the one who struck him does not carry the guilt of shedding blood.

decisions.choice: verse numbers: Hebrew 22:1 is 22:2 in many Bibles
decisions.reason: This translation numbers verses as the Hebrew text does. The Hebrew text ends chapter 21 one verse later than many Bibles, so Hebrew 21:37 is 22:1 there, and Hebrew 22:1-30 is 22:2-31. The words are the same; only the numbers differ.

decisions.choice: breaking in: digging or forcing a way through a house wall
decisions.reason: The word comes from a verb meaning to dig through. Houses were built of mud brick, and a thief could break through the wall (Jeremiah 2:34 uses the same word). The thief is caught in the act.

decisions.choice: no blood for him: no guilt for shedding his blood
decisions.reason: "Blood" (plural) here means guilt for blood that was shed, as in Deuteronomy 19:10. The householder who strikes a burglar in the dark does not bear guilt for the thief's death. Verse 2 sets the limit.

decisions.choice: at night
decisions.reason: The contrast with "if the sun has risen" in verse 2 shows that the break-in happens in the dark. Readable says "at night"; Literal and Balanced leave it to verse 2.

records.heading: Theft and damage to property

records.source: אִם־זָרְחָ֥ה הַשֶּׁ֛מֶשׁ עָלָ֖יו דָּמִ֣ים ל֑וֹ שַׁלֵּ֣ם יְשַׁלֵּ֔ם אִם־אֵ֣ין ל֔וֹ וְנִמְכַּ֖ר בִּגְנֵבָתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: If has risen the sun on him, blood[s] for him. Surely he will make restitution; if there is not to him, and he will be sold for his theft.
pieces: But if the sun is already up when it happens, the killing brings bloodguilt. The thief must repay in full; if he owns nothing, he is to be sold to make up for what he took.

L.2: If the sun has risen on him, [there is] blood[guilt] for him. He shall surely make restitution; if he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft.

R.2: But if the sun is up, the one who kills the thief is guilty of shedding blood. A thief has to repay what he took. If he owns nothing, he will be sold as a slave, and the price will cover what he stole.

decisions.choice: the sun has risen on him: the break-in happens in daylight
decisions.reason: By day the householder can see who the intruder is, call for help and bring the thief to account; killing him then is not self-defense in the dark but shedding blood. "On him" may refer to the thief or to the householder; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: he shall surely make restitution: the thief, who was not killed
decisions.reason: The subject moves back to the thief. A thief who is caught alive must repay what he took, as verse 3 and 21:37 set out.

decisions.choice: sold for his theft: sold as a slave to pay what he owes
decisions.reason: A thief who cannot pay is sold, and the price of his labor goes to repay the loss. The laws of 21:2-6 govern a Hebrew slave.

decisions.choice: as a slave ... the price will cover what he stole
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what being sold means and why it is done. "Slave" stays, as the style guide keeps it where people are sold (21:2).

records.source: אִֽם־הִמָּצֵא֩ תִמָּצֵ֨א בְיָד֜וֹ הַגְּנֵבָ֗ה מִשּׁ֧וֹר עַד־חֲמ֛וֹר עַד־שֶׂ֖ה חַיִּ֑ים שְׁנַ֖יִם יְשַׁלֵּֽם׃ס
records.gloss: If indeed it is found in his hand the stolen thing, from ox to donkey to sheep, alive, double he will make restitution.
pieces: Should the animal he stole, whether an ox, a donkey or a sheep, still be alive and in his hands when it is found, he must repay double.

L.3: If the stolen [animal] is indeed found in his hand, whether ox or donkey or sheep, alive, he shall repay double.

R.3: If the thief still has the ox, donkey or sheep he stole, and it is alive, he must give the owner two animals for every one he took.

decisions.choice: double: the stolen animal returned and as much again
decisions.reason: The thief gives back twice what he took. An ox or sheep already slaughtered or sold was repaid more heavily, fivefold and fourfold (21:37), since the thief could no longer return it.

decisions.choice: in his hand: in his possession
decisions.reason: "Hand" often means a person's power or keeping.

decisions.choice: two animals for every one he took
decisions.reason: Readable shows what "double" means in practice and names the owner who receives it.

records.source: כִּ֤י יַבְעֶר־אִישׁ֙ שָׂדֶ֣ה אוֹ־כֶ֔רֶם וְשִׁלַּח֙ אֶת־בְּעִיר֔וֹ וּבִעֵ֖ר בִּשְׂדֵ֣ה אַחֵ֑ר מֵיטַ֥ב שָׂדֵ֛הוּ וּמֵיטַ֥ב כַּרְמ֖וֹ יְשַׁלֵּֽם׃ס
records.gloss: When causes to be grazed anyone a field or a vineyard, and lets loose his cattle, and it grazes in [the] field of another, [the] best of his field and [the] best of his vineyard he will make compensation.
pieces: Suppose {{gender:someone|a man}} turns animals out to graze a field or a vineyard, and lets them loose so that they feed in another person's field. Then the best that {{gender:their|his}} own field and vineyard produce must be used to repay the loss.

L.4: If {{gender:someone|a man}} causes a field or a vineyard to be grazed over, and lets loose {{gender:their|his}} animals, and it grazes in the field of another, [from] the best of {{gender:their|his}} field and the best of {{gender:their|his}} vineyard {{gender:they|he}} shall make restitution.

R.4: {{gender:Someone|A man}} might let {{gender:their|his}} animals graze in a field or vineyard, and the animals might wander into another person's field and eat there. Then the owner of the animals must pay for the damage with the best crops from {{gender:their|his}} own field or vineyard.

decisions.choice: cause to be grazed: let animals feed
alternatives: If someone burns a field or vineyard, and lets the fire loose
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to graze or to burn; the two senses share a form, and verse 5 uses the same root for fire. Read as grazing, this law is about stray livestock; read as burning, it is about a fire set in a field, and verse 5 goes on to a fire that spreads. The mention of "his cattle" favors grazing.

decisions.choice: the shorter Hebrew text
decisions.reason: Some ancient witnesses, including the Samaritan Pentateuch and the old Greek translation, have a longer text: he repays from his own field according to its yield, and if the animals grazed the whole field, he repays from the best of his field and vineyard. The Hebrew text has only the second part.

decisions.choice: from the best: the loss is made up with the best of his own produce
decisions.reason: The one at fault does not repay with poor produce. He gives the best of what his own land yields.

decisions.choice: the owner of the animals ... pay for the damage
decisions.reason: Readable names who pays and calls the loss "the damage".

records.source: כִּֽי־תֵצֵ֨א אֵ֜שׁ וּמָצְאָ֤ה קֹצִים֙ וְנֶאֱכַ֣ל גָּדִ֔ישׁ א֥וֹ הַקָּמָ֖ה א֣וֹ הַשָּׂדֶ֑ה שַׁלֵּ֣ם יְשַׁלֵּ֔ם הַמַּבְעִ֖ר אֶת־הַבְּעֵרָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: When goes out fire and finds thorns, and is consumed a stack of sheaves or the standing grain or the field, surely he will make compensation, the one who kindled the fire.
pieces: Suppose a fire is lit, and it catches in the thorns and spreads, and stacked grain, grain still standing, or a whole field burns up. The person who lit the fire must pay in full for the loss.

L.5: If fire goes out and finds thorns, and a stack of sheaves or the standing grain or the field is consumed, the one who kindled the blaze shall surely make restitution.

R.5: Someone might light a fire that spreads into the thornbushes and burns up another person's grain, whether it is stacked or still growing in the field. The person who lit it must pay back the whole loss.

decisions.choice: fire finds thorns: a fire that spreads through brush
decisions.reason: Thornbushes grew along the edges of fields and were burned to clear land. A fire lit for that purpose could catch in them and run on into a neighbor's grain.

decisions.choice: stacked grain ... standing grain
decisions.reason: The first is grain already cut and piled in sheaves; the second is grain not yet harvested. Either way the harvest is lost.

decisions.choice: the one who kindled: the one responsible, even without intent
decisions.reason: The person who lit the fire repays, though he did not mean the fire to spread. Carelessness with fire is a wrong to the neighbor.

decisions.choice: another person's grain
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the loss is a neighbor's.

records.source: כִּֽי־יִתֵּן֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֜הוּ כֶּ֤סֶף אֽוֹ־כֵלִים֙ לִשְׁמֹ֔ר וְגֻנַּ֖ב מִבֵּ֣ית הָאִ֑ישׁ אִם־יִמָּצֵ֥א הַגַּנָּ֖ב יְשַׁלֵּ֥ם שְׁנָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: When gives anyone to his neighbor money or articles to keep, and it is stolen from the house of the person, if is found the thief, he will make restitution double.
pieces: Suppose {{gender:someone|a man}} hands money or other things over to a neighbor to look after, and a thief takes them from that house. If the thief is found, he must repay twice the value.

L.6: If {{gender:someone|a man}} gives to {{gender:their|his}} neighbor money or articles to keep, and it is stolen from the {{gender:person's|man's}} house, if the thief is found, he shall repay double.

R.6: {{gender:Someone|A man}} might leave money or valuables with a neighbor to keep safe, and then a thief breaks into the neighbor's house and takes them. If they find the thief, he has to pay back twice as much.

decisions.choice: money or articles: silver or goods
decisions.reason: The word for money is "silver", which was weighed out as payment. "Articles" covers belongings of any kind: tools, vessels, clothing.

decisions.choice: the house of the person: the house of the neighbor who kept the goods
decisions.reason: The goods are stolen while in the keeper's care. If the thief is caught, he pays double, as in verse 3; verses 7-8 deal with the case where he is not found.

records.heading: Things left in a neighbor's care

records.source: אִם־לֹ֤א יִמָּצֵא֙ הַגַּנָּ֔ב וְנִקְרַ֥ב בַּֽעַל־הַבַּ֖יִת אֶל־הָֽאֱלֹהִ֑ים אִם־לֹ֥א שָׁלַ֛ח יָד֖וֹ בִּמְלֶ֥אכֶת רֵעֵֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: If is not found the thief, and will be brought near the master of the house to God, [to see] if not he has stretched out his hand on the property of his neighbor.
pieces: If the thief is not found, the owner of the house is to come before God and declare that he did not lay a hand on his neighbor's goods.

L.7: If the thief is not found, the master of the house shall be brought near to God, [to swear] that he has not stretched out his hand to his neighbor's property.

R.7: If the thief is not caught, the owner of the house must stand before God. There he must swear that he did not take his neighbor's things himself.

decisions.choice: God: God himself, before whom the case is brought
decisions.reason: To come near to God means to come to the sanctuary to have the matter judged before him. Some read the word here as "the judges", who heard cases at the sanctuary in God's name. The word is the usual one for God, and the case is settled by God's verdict or by an oath sworn in his name (verse 10). In verse 8 the verb "condemns" is plural, which may point to judges, though the word for God also takes a plural verb at times (Genesis 20:13; 35:7). Compare 21:6.

decisions.choice: whether he has not: the words of an oath of innocence
decisions.reason: "If not" is the form oaths take in Hebrew: "(may God judge me) if I did not ...", that is, "I swear that I did not". The keeper swears that he did not take the goods himself; verse 10 speaks of the oath outright.

decisions.choice: stretch out his hand to: take or misuse
decisions.reason: To put one's hand to someone's goods is to help oneself to them.

records.source: עַֽל־כָּל־דְּבַר־פֶּ֡שַׁע עַל־שׁ֡וֹר עַל־חֲ֠מוֹר עַל־שֶׂ֨ה עַל־שַׂלְמָ֜ה עַל־כָּל־אֲבֵדָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר יֹאמַר֙ כִּי־ה֣וּא זֶ֔ה עַ֚ד הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים יָבֹ֖א דְּבַר־שְׁנֵיהֶ֑ם אֲשֶׁ֤ר יַרְשִׁיעֻן֙ אֱלֹהִ֔ים יְשַׁלֵּ֥ם שְׁנַ֖יִם לְרֵעֵֽהוּ׃ס
records.gloss: On every matter of transgression, on an ox, on a donkey, on a sheep, on a garment, on every lost thing of which one says, this is it, to God will come the case of both of them; [the one] whom condemns God will make restitution double to his neighbor.
pieces: Whenever there is a charge of wrongdoing over an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a cloak or anything lost, and someone claims, 'This is it,' the two of them shall take their case to God. The one whom God condemns must repay {{gender:their|his}} neighbor double.

L.8: For every matter of transgression, for ox, for donkey, for sheep, for garment, for any lost thing of which one says, 'This is it,' the case of the two of them shall come to God; [the one] whom God condemns shall repay double to {{gender:their|his}} neighbor.

R.8: Two people may quarrel over an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a piece of clothing or some lost thing, with one of them saying, 'This is mine.' They must take the quarrel to God, and whoever God says is in the wrong must give the other person twice what it is worth.

decisions.choice: matter of transgression: a charge of wrongful taking
decisions.reason: The word often means rebellion or breaking faith. Here it is a breach of trust over property: one party says the other has taken what is not his.

decisions.choice: this is it: the claim that the thing found is the one that was lost
decisions.reason: The owner recognizes the missing item and says so. The words may mean "This is mine" or "This is the one".

decisions.choice: God ... the one whom God condemns
alternatives: the judges ... the one whom the judges condemn
decisions.reason: The case is decided before God, and the one he finds guilty pays. Some read the word here as "the judges", who heard cases at the sanctuary in God's name. The word is the usual one for God, and the case is settled by God's verdict or by an oath sworn in his name (verse 10). In verse 8 the verb "condemns" is plural, which may point to judges, though the word for God also takes a plural verb at times (Genesis 20:13; 35:7). Compare 21:6.

decisions.choice: whoever God says is in the wrong
decisions.reason: Readable puts "condemns" in everyday words.

records.source: כִּֽי־יִתֵּן֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֜הוּ חֲמ֨וֹר אוֹ־שׁ֥וֹר אוֹ־שֶׂ֛ה וְכָל־בְּהֵמָ֖ה לִשְׁמֹ֑ר וּמֵ֛ת אוֹ־נִשְׁבַּ֥ר אוֹ־נִשְׁבָּ֖ה אֵ֥ין רֹאֶֽה׃
records.gloss: When gives anyone to his neighbor a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any animal to keep, and it dies or is maimed or is captured, there is no one seeing,
pieces: Suppose {{gender:someone|a man}} entrusts a donkey, an ox, a sheep or any other animal to a neighbor's care, and it dies, is hurt or is carried off when no one is there to see.

L.9: If {{gender:someone|a man}} gives to {{gender:their|his}} neighbor a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any animal to keep, and it dies or is injured or is carried off, [and] no one sees [it],

R.9: {{gender:Someone|A man}} might ask a neighbor to take care of a donkey, an ox, a sheep or some other animal. Then the animal might die, get hurt or be taken by raiders while no one is watching.

decisions.choice: injured: broken, maimed
decisions.reason: The verb means to break, as of a broken leg that leaves an animal lame or useless.

decisions.choice: captured: carried off by raiders
decisions.reason: This is the word for taking captives in war. The animal is driven off by a band of raiders, a loss the keeper could not prevent (compare Job 1:15, 17).

decisions.choice: no one seeing: no witness to say what happened
decisions.reason: Since no one else can tell how the animal was lost, the matter is settled by an oath (verse 10).

decisions.choice: taken by raiders
decisions.reason: Readable names who carries the animal off.

records.source: שְׁבֻעַ֣ת יְהוָ֗ה תִּהְיֶה֙ בֵּ֣ין שְׁנֵיהֶ֔ם אִם־לֹ֥א שָׁלַ֛ח יָד֖וֹ בִּמְלֶ֣אכֶת רֵעֵ֑הוּ וְלָקַ֥ח בְּעָלָ֖יו וְלֹ֥א יְשַׁלֵּֽם׃
records.gloss: An oath of Yahweh will be between the two of them, if not he has stretched out his hand on the property of his neighbor; and will accept [it] its owner, and not he will make compensation.
pieces: Then the two of them shall settle it with an oath of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: the one who kept the animal swears to having taken none of the neighbor's property. The owner must accept the oath, and nothing has to be paid back.

L.10: an oath of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} shall be between the two of them, [that] {{gender:they|he}} did not stretch out {{gender:their|his}} hand to {{gender:their|his}} neighbor's property; and its owner shall accept [it], and {{gender:they|he}} shall not make restitution.

R.10: In that case, the neighbor must swear by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, in front of the owner, that the animal was not taken by the neighbor. The owner must accept this oath. The neighbor does not have to pay anything back.

decisions.choice: an oath of Yahweh: an oath sworn in Yahweh's name
decisions.reason: The keeper calls on God as witness. One who swore falsely would answer to God, who will not hold guiltless anyone who takes his name in vain (20:7).

decisions.choice: that he did not: the words of the oath
decisions.reason: As in verse 7, "if not" is the form of an oath: the keeper swears that he did not take the animal for himself.

decisions.choice: its owner shall accept: accept the oath as settling the matter
decisions.reason: The verb means to take. Most likely the owner takes the oath as the end of the dispute. It may instead mean that the owner takes what is left of the animal.

records.source: וְאִם־גָּנֹ֥ב יִגָּנֵ֖ב מֵעִמּ֑וֹ יְשַׁלֵּ֖ם לִבְעָלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And if indeed it is stolen from with him, he will make restitution to its owner.
pieces: But if the animal was actually stolen from the one keeping it, that person must repay its owner.

L.11: But if it is indeed stolen from {{gender:them|him}}, {{gender:they|he}} shall make restitution to its owner.

R.11: But if a thief stole the animal while the neighbor was caring for it, the neighbor must pay the owner for it.

decisions.choice: stolen from him: taken while in his care
decisions.reason: A theft from the keeper's own place is something he should have guarded against, unlike raiders or death (verse 9). So he makes the loss good.

decisions.choice: the one keeping it / the neighbor
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the keeper instead of using "him".

records.source: אִם־טָרֹ֥ף יִטָּרֵ֖ף יְבִאֵ֣הוּ עֵ֑ד הַטְּרֵפָ֖ה לֹ֥א יְשַׁלֵּֽם׃פ
records.gloss: If indeed it is torn in pieces, he will bring it [as] evidence; the torn animal not he will make restitution.
pieces: If beasts tore it to pieces, the keeper is to bring what is left as evidence and owes nothing for the animal that was torn.

L.12: If it is indeed torn in pieces, {{gender:they|he}} shall bring it [as] evidence; [for] the torn [animal] {{gender:they|he}} shall not make restitution.

R.12: If a wild animal killed it, the neighbor must bring what is left of the body to show what happened. Then the neighbor does not have to pay for it.

decisions.choice: torn: killed by a wild animal
decisions.reason: The verb is used of a lion or wolf tearing its prey (Genesis 37:33; 49:27). Jacob bore the loss of animals torn by beasts himself (Genesis 31:39); this law lets the keeper go free.

decisions.choice: bring it as evidence: show the remains
decisions.reason: The remains prove the animal was not stolen or sold. Amos 3:12 pictures a shepherd rescuing two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth, as proof of this kind.

decisions.choice: the keeper / the neighbor ... what is left
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the keeper and say what is brought: the remains of the animal.

records.source: וְכִֽי־יִשְׁאַ֥ל אִ֛ישׁ מֵעִ֥ם רֵעֵ֖הוּ וְנִשְׁבַּ֣ר אוֹ־מֵ֑ת בְּעָלָ֥יו אֵין־עִמּ֖וֹ שַׁלֵּ֥ם יְשַׁלֵּֽם׃
records.gloss: And when asks anyone from with his neighbor, and it is maimed or dies, its owner not with it, surely he will make restitution.
pieces: {{gender:Anyone|A man}} who borrows a neighbor's animal must make full repayment if it is hurt or dies while its owner is absent.

L.13: And if {{gender:someone|a man}} asks [an animal] from {{gender:their|his}} neighbor, and it is injured or dies, its owner not [being] with it, {{gender:they|he}} shall surely make restitution.

R.13: {{gender:Someone|A man}} might borrow a neighbor's animal, and it gets hurt or dies while the owner is not with it. Then the borrower has to pay the owner for it.

decisions.choice: asks: borrows
decisions.reason: This is the verb of 3:22, 11:2 and 12:35, where Israel asked the Egyptians for silver and gold as a gift. In this law about loss and repayment it means to ask for the use of something, that is, to borrow.

decisions.choice: its owner not with it: the owner was not there to look after it
decisions.reason: When the owner is absent, the borrower is responsible for the animal and must pay for any harm.

decisions.choice: animal
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not say what is borrowed; the next words show it is an animal, as in verse 9. Literal supplies it in brackets.

records.source: אִם־בְּעָלָ֥יו עִמּ֖וֹ לֹ֣א יְשַׁלֵּ֑ם אִם־שָׂכִ֣יר ה֔וּא בָּ֖א בִּשְׂכָרֽוֹ׃ס
records.gloss: If its owner [was] with it, not he will make restitution; if a hired thing it [was], it came for its hire.
pieces: But if the owner was present, there is no repayment. If the animal was rented, the owner's loss is met by the rent.

L.14: If its owner [was] with it, {{gender:they|he}} shall not make restitution; if it [was] hired, it came for its hire.

R.14: But if the owner was there, the borrower does not have to pay anything. If the animal was rented for money, the money paid for its use is all the owner gets.

decisions.choice: its owner with it: present and able to look after it
decisions.reason: If the owner was there, the loss is his own, since he could have protected the animal.

decisions.choice: it came for its hire: the fee paid covers the risk
alternatives: if he was a hired worker, it is counted against his wages
decisions.reason: A rented animal was paid for, and the owner took the risk of loss in return for the fee. The word for "hired" is used elsewhere of a hired worker (12:45), so it may mean: if the borrower was a hired man, the loss is counted against his wages.

records.source: וְכִֽי־יְפַתֶּ֣ה אִ֗ישׁ בְּתוּלָ֛ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹא־אֹרָ֖שָׂה וְשָׁכַ֣ב עִמָּ֑הּ מָהֹ֛ר יִמְהָרֶ֥נָּה לּ֖וֹ לְאִשָּֽׁה׃
records.gloss: And when seduces a man a virgin who not was betrothed, and he lies with her, surely he will pay the bride-price for her for himself as a wife.
pieces: If a man talks a virgin who is not betrothed into lying with him, he must pay the price paid for a bride and take her as his wife.

L.15: And if a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed, and lies with her, he shall surely pay the mohar for her [to make her] his wife.

R.15: Suppose a man talks a young woman into sleeping with him. If she is a virgin and is not engaged, he must pay her father the price for a bride and marry her.

decisions.choice: seduces: persuades, entices
decisions.reason: The verb means to persuade or lure. This is a case of seduction, not of force; Deuteronomy 22:28-29 deals with a man who seizes a young woman.

decisions.choice: the bride-price: the payment a bridegroom gave the bride's family
decisions.reason: When a marriage was agreed, the bridegroom paid a sum to the bride's father (Genesis 34:12; 1 Samuel 18:25). The man who seduces a virgin must do what a bridegroom does and marry her.

decisions.choice: not betrothed: not yet pledged in marriage
decisions.reason: Betrothal was a binding agreement to marry, and a betrothed woman was treated almost as a wife (Deuteronomy 22:23-24). This law is about a young woman not yet promised to anyone.

decisions.choice: the price paid for a bride / the price for a bride
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew name for the payment. Balanced and Readable say what it is. Readable also names her father, who receives it (verse 16).

records.heading: A seduced virgin

records.source: אִם־מָאֵ֧ן יְמָאֵ֛ן אָבִ֖יהָ לְתִתָּ֣הּ ל֑וֹ כֶּ֣סֶף יִשְׁקֹ֔ל כְּמֹ֖הַר הַבְּתוּלֹֽת׃ס
records.gloss: If utterly refuses her father to give her to him, silver he will weigh out according to the bride-price of virgins.
pieces: Should her father flatly refuse to let him marry her, the man must still weigh out silver equal to the price paid for a virgin bride.

L.16: If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall weigh out silver according to the mohar of virgins.

R.16: Her father may refuse to let the man marry her. Even so, the man has to pay the father as much silver as is given for a bride who is a virgin.

decisions.choice: weigh out silver: pay in silver by weight
decisions.reason: There were no coins. Silver was weighed on scales to make a payment (Genesis 23:16).

decisions.choice: her father utterly refuses: the father keeps the right to refuse
decisions.reason: The doubled verb makes the refusal firm. The father decides whether the marriage goes ahead; the man pays either way.

decisions.choice: the man
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the man who pays, since "he" could be read as the father.

records.source: מְכַשֵּׁפָ֖ה לֹ֥א תְחַיֶּֽה׃ס
records.gloss: A sorceress not you will let live.
pieces: You shall not let a sorceress live.

L.17: A sorceress you shall not let live.

R.17: A woman who uses magic spells must be put to death.

decisions.choice: sorceress: a woman who practices magic
decisions.reason: The word is the feminine form of the one used for Pharaoh's sorcerers (7:11), who worked spells and tried to match God's signs. The feminine may reflect who most often practiced it; the ban on sorcery itself applies to all (Deuteronomy 18:10; Leviticus 20:27 names "a man or a woman").

decisions.choice: not let live: sorcery is a capital crime
decisions.reason: Magic sought hidden power apart from God and was an offense against him, not only against a neighbor.

decisions.choice: must be put to death
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "not let live" means.

records.heading: Death penalties and care for the weak

records.source: כָּל־שֹׁכֵ֥ב עִם־בְּהֵמָ֖ה מ֥וֹת יוּמָֽת׃ס
records.gloss: Anyone lying with an animal surely will be put to death.
pieces: Death is the penalty for anyone who lies with an animal.

L.18: Anyone lying with an animal shall surely be put to death.

R.18: If someone has sex with an animal, that person must be put to death.

decisions.choice: lie with: have sexual relations with
decisions.reason: The same law appears in Leviticus 18:23 and 20:15-16, where it covers men and women alike.

decisions.choice: surely be put to death
decisions.reason: The doubled verb is the strong form used for the gravest crimes in these laws (21:12, 15-17).

records.source: זֹבֵ֥חַ לָאֱלֹהִ֖ים יָֽחֳרָ֑ם בִּלְתִּ֥י לַיהוָ֖ה לְבַדּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: One sacrificing to the gods will be devoted to destruction, except to Yahweh alone.
pieces: Anyone who offers sacrifice to other gods, and not to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} alone, shall be devoted to destruction.

L.19: [One] sacrificing to [the] gods shall be devoted to destruction, except to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} alone.

R.19: Offer sacrifices only to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Anyone who sacrifices to other gods must be completely destroyed.

decisions.choice: devoted to destruction: given over wholly to God by being destroyed
decisions.reason: The verb describes something set apart for God so completely that it may not be kept or ransomed, but must be destroyed (Leviticus 27:29). Deuteronomy 13:13-19 applies it to a town that turns to other gods. One who worships other gods is put to death.

decisions.choice: gods ... except Yahweh alone
decisions.reason: The word for God is plural here and means other gods, as in 20:3. Sacrifice belongs to Yahweh and no one else.

decisions.choice: Offer sacrifices only to the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable puts the command to sacrifice to the LORD alone first, then the penalty.

records.source: וְגֵ֥ר לֹא־תוֹנֶ֖ה וְלֹ֣א תִלְחָצֶ֑נּוּ כִּֽי־גֵרִ֥ים הֱיִיתֶ֖ם בְּאֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And a sojourner not you must maltreat, and not you must oppress him, for sojourners you were in the land of Egypt.
pieces: Do no wrong to a foreigner living among you, and do not oppress anyone like that, because you yourselves lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt.

L.20: And a sojourner you shall not wrong, and you shall not oppress {{gender:them|him}}, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.

R.20: Never be unkind or unfair to a foreigner living among you. After all, you were once foreigners in the land of Egypt.

decisions.choice: sojourner: a foreigner living among Israel
decisions.reason: A sojourner was someone from elsewhere who lived among a people without family land or relatives to protect him (12:48-49; 23:9).

decisions.choice: wrong ... oppress: cheat, and press hard
decisions.reason: The first verb is used of cheating in buying and selling (Leviticus 25:14). The second means to squeeze; it is the word for the oppression the Egyptians laid on Israel (3:9).

decisions.choice: for you were sojourners in Egypt: Israel's own past as the reason
decisions.reason: Israel knows what it is to be a foreigner under oppression, so they must not treat others as Egypt treated them (23:9; Leviticus 19:34; Deuteronomy 10:19).

decisions.choice: foreigner living among you / foreigners
decisions.reason: As in 12:48-49, Balanced and Readable say "foreigner living among you" for "sojourner", which Literal keeps.

records.source: כָּל־אַלְמָנָ֥ה וְיָת֖וֹם לֹ֥א תְעַנּֽוּן׃
records.gloss: Any widow and a fatherless one not you must afflict.
pieces: You shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child.

L.21: Any widow or fatherless [child] you shall not afflict.

R.21: Never be cruel to a widow or to a child whose father has died.

decisions.choice: widow and fatherless: those left without a husband or father to provide for them
decisions.reason: A widow had lost her husband and a fatherless child his father, though the mother might be living. Without a man to stand up for them they were easily wronged, and God takes up their cause (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17).

decisions.choice: afflict: mistreat, humble
decisions.reason: This is the verb used of the Egyptians who afflicted Israel with forced labor (1:11-12).

records.source: אִם־עַנֵּ֥ה תְעַנֶּ֖ה אֹת֑וֹ כִּ֣י אִם־צָעֹ֤ק יִצְעַק֙ אֵלַ֔י שָׁמֹ֥עַ אֶשְׁמַ֖ע צַעֲקָתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: If indeed you afflict him, for if indeed he cries out to me, surely I will hear his cry,
pieces: Should you afflict them, you can be sure that when they cry out to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, I will hear their cry,

L.22: If you indeed afflict {{gender:them|him}}, then should {{gender:they|he}} indeed cry out to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, I will surely hear {{gender:their|his}} cry,

R.22: If you treat them badly, they will call to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} for help, and I will certainly hear them.

decisions.choice: indeed afflict ... indeed cry out ... surely hear
decisions.reason: Each verb is doubled for emphasis: any wrong done to them at all, any cry at all, will certainly be heard. The "if" has its outcome in verse 23.

decisions.choice: I will surely hear his cry: as God heard Israel in Egypt
decisions.reason: God heard the cry of Israel under their slave masters and came down to rescue them (2:23-24; 3:7). He will hear the widow and the fatherless in the same way.

records.source: וְחָרָ֣ה אַפִּ֔י וְהָרַגְתִּ֥י אֶתְכֶ֖ם בֶּחָ֑רֶב וְהָי֤וּ נְשֵׁיכֶם֙ אַלְמָנ֔וֹת וּבְנֵיכֶ֖ם יְתֹמִֽים׃פ
records.gloss: And will burn my anger, and I will kill you with the sword, and will be your wives widows and your children fatherless.
pieces: and {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} wrath will burn, and I will put you to death by the sword; your own wives will then be widows, and your children will have no fathers.

L.23: and {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} anger will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives will be widows and your children fatherless.

R.23: Then I will become very angry. I will kill you in war, and your wives will become widows, and your children will lose their fathers.

decisions.choice: my anger will burn: I will be fiercely angry
decisions.reason: Anger is pictured as fire that flares up (4:14; 32:10-11).

decisions.choice: your wives widows and your children fatherless: the punishment fits the wrong
decisions.reason: Those who mistreat widows and the fatherless will leave their own wives widowed and their own children fatherless.

decisions.choice: in war
decisions.reason: Death "by the sword" means death in battle. Readable says so.

records.source: אִם־כֶּ֣סֶף׀תַּלְוֶ֣ה אֶת־עַמִּ֗י אֶת־הֶֽעָנִי֙ עִמָּ֔ךְ לֹא־תִהְיֶ֥ה ל֖וֹ כְּנֹשֶׁ֑ה לֹֽא־תְשִׂימ֥וּן עָלָ֖יו נֶֽשֶׁךְ׃
records.gloss: If money you lend to my people, to the poor with you, not you must be to him like a creditor; not you must put on him interest.
pieces: When you lend money to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, to a poor person living near you, do not deal with that person as a creditor would, and do not make them pay interest.

L.24: If you lend money to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, to the poor [one] with you, you shall not be to {{gender:them|him}} like a creditor; you shall not lay interest on {{gender:them|him}}.

R.24: Suppose you lend money to a poor person among {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people. Do not be a hard lender who demands payment, and lend it without interest.

decisions.choice: interest: a charge added to a loan
decisions.reason: A loan to a poor neighbor was help in hard times, not a way to make a profit from need. Leviticus 25:35-37 gives the same rule.

decisions.choice: creditor: one who presses a debtor to repay
decisions.reason: The word is used of a lender who comes to collect, even by taking the debtor's children as slaves (2 Kings 4:1).

decisions.choice: my people, the poor with you
decisions.reason: The second phrase explains the first: the borrower is one of God's own people who is poor and lives among you.

records.heading: Lending to the poor

records.source: אִם־חָבֹ֥ל תַּחְבֹּ֖ל שַׂלְמַ֣ת רֵעֶ֑ךָ עַד־בֹּ֥א הַשֶּׁ֖מֶשׁ תְּשִׁיבֶ֥נּוּ לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: If indeed you take as pledge the cloak of your neighbor, by the going of the sun you will return it to him,
pieces: Should you hold your neighbor's cloak as a pledge for a debt, you must hand it back to its owner before sunset,

L.25: If you indeed take your neighbor's cloak as a pledge, by the going of the sun you shall return it to {{gender:them|him}},

R.25: Your neighbor may give you a coat to hold as a promise to repay a loan. If so, you must return it by evening.

decisions.choice: take as a pledge: hold something as security for a loan
decisions.reason: A lender could keep an item of the borrower's until the loan was repaid. Deuteronomy 24:10-13 adds that the lender must not go into the house to take it.

decisions.choice: by the going of the sun: before sunset
decisions.reason: The cloak must be back with its owner before night falls, for the reason given in verse 26.

records.source: כִּ֣י הִ֤וא כְסוּתוֹ֙ לְבַדָּ֔הּ הִ֥וא שִׂמְלָת֖וֹ לְעֹר֑וֹ בַּמֶּ֣ה יִשְׁכָּ֔ב וְהָיָה֙ כִּֽי־יִצְעַ֣ק אֵלַ֔י וְשָׁמַעְתִּ֖י כִּֽי־חַנּ֥וּן אָֽנִי׃ס
records.gloss: for it [is] his covering, it alone; it [is] his cloak for his skin. In what will he lie down? And it will be, when he cries out to me, I will hear, for gracious I [am].
pieces: for it is the only covering {{gender:they have|he has}}, the cloak that wraps {{gender:their|his}} body. In what will {{gender:they|he}} lie down to sleep? When that neighbor cries out to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, I will hear, because I am gracious.

L.26: for it [is] {{gender:their|his}} only covering; it [is] {{gender:their|his}} cloak for {{gender:their|his}} skin. In what will {{gender:they|he}} lie down? And it shall be, should {{gender:they|he}} cry out to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, I will hear, for I [am] gracious.

R.26: That coat is all your neighbor has to keep warm. Without it, what will your neighbor sleep under? If your neighbor calls to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} for help, I will listen, because I am kind and full of mercy.

decisions.choice: his only covering, his cloak for his skin: the outer garment that served as a blanket
decisions.reason: The cloak was a large outer garment worn by day and slept in at night. A poor person might own nothing else to keep warm (Deuteronomy 24:12-13).

decisions.choice: in what will he lie down?: he will have nothing to sleep in
decisions.reason: The question expects no answer; it makes the hardship plain.

decisions.choice: I am gracious: God's own character
decisions.reason: The word describes kindness and favor freely given to those in need. God names himself this way when he shows Moses his glory (34:6).

decisions.choice: kind and full of mercy
decisions.reason: Readable spells out "gracious" in plain words.

records.source: אֱלֹהִ֖ים לֹ֣א תְקַלֵּ֑ל וְנָשִׂ֥יא בְעַמְּךָ֖ לֹ֥א תָאֹֽר׃
records.gloss: God not you must curse, and a leader among your people not you must curse.
pieces: Do not speak contemptuously of God, and do not call down a curse on a leader of your people.

L.27: God you shall not revile, and a leader among your people you shall not curse.

R.27: Do not speak against God with disrespect, and do not ask for evil to happen to a leader of your people.

decisions.choice: God: God himself
decisions.reason: The word is the usual one for God. Set beside "a leader among your people", it may instead mean the judges, as some read it in verses 7-8 and in 21:6. Paul quotes the second half of the verse of the high priest (Acts 23:5).

decisions.choice: revile: treat with contempt, speak lightly of
decisions.reason: The verb means to make light of someone or curse them. Leviticus 24:15-16 sets the penalty for one who curses God.

decisions.choice: leader: a chief or head among the people
decisions.reason: The word is used of the leaders of the congregation (16:22; 34:31), the heads of Israel's tribes and clans.

records.heading: Firstfruits and firstborn

records.source: מְלֵאָתְךָ֥ וְדִמְעֲךָ֖ לֹ֣א תְאַחֵ֑ר בְּכ֥וֹר בָּנֶ֖יךָ תִּתֶּן־לִּֽי׃
records.gloss: Your fullness and your juice not you must delay. The firstborn of your sons you will give to me.
pieces: Do not be slow to give from the abundance of your harvest or from what flows from your presses. Your firstborn sons you shall give to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

L.28: Your fullness and your outflow you shall not delay. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.28: Do not wait to bring {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} the first part of your grain, your wine and your olive oil. Give {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} your oldest sons.

decisions.choice: your fullness and your outflow: the full yield of the harvest and the juice of the presses
alternatives: your first grain and your first wine
decisions.reason: Both words are rare, and the sense is uncertain. "Fullness" most likely means the ripe grain, and "outflow" what runs from the wine and olive presses. The command is not to hold back God's share of them, probably the firstfruits (23:19).

decisions.choice: the firstborn of your sons you shall give to me
decisions.reason: The firstborn belong to God because he spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt (13:2, 15). Firstborn sons were given to God by being redeemed (13:13; 34:20), not by sacrifice.

decisions.choice: me ... the first part ... your wine and your olive oil
decisions.reason: Readable says to whom the produce is brought and names what flows from the presses. This spells out a rare and uncertain phrase.

decisions.choice: oldest sons
decisions.reason: As in 11:5, Readable says "oldest son" for "firstborn".

records.source: כֵּֽן־תַּעֲשֶׂ֥ה לְשֹׁרְךָ֖ לְצֹאנֶ֑ךָ שִׁבְעַ֤ת יָמִים֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה עִם־אִמּ֔וֹ בַּיּ֥וֹם הַשְּׁמִינִ֖י תִּתְּנוֹ־לִֽי׃
records.gloss: Thus you will do to your ox, to your sheep: seven days it will be with its mother; on the eighth day you will give it to me.
pieces: You are to do likewise with your oxen and your sheep: for seven days the firstborn remains with its mother, and on the eighth day you shall give it to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

L.29: Thus you shall do with your ox, with your sheep: seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.29: Do this also with the firstborn of your cattle and sheep. Each one should stay with its mother for a week, and on the eighth day you must give it to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: thus you shall do: the firstborn of the herd and flock also belong to God
decisions.reason: "Thus" looks back to the firstborn sons of verse 28. The firstborn males of the animals are given to God as well (13:12).

decisions.choice: seven days with its mother, given on the eighth
decisions.reason: A newborn animal was not offered until it was eight days old (Leviticus 22:27).

decisions.choice: sheep: a sheep or a goat
decisions.reason: The word covers one animal of the flock, sheep or goat (12:5).

decisions.choice: the firstborn
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say that it is the firstborn animal, which the Hebrew leaves to the context.

records.source: וְאַנְשֵׁי־קֹ֖דֶשׁ תִּהְי֣וּן לִ֑י וּבָשָׂ֨ר בַּשָּׂדֶ֤ה טְרֵפָה֙ לֹ֣א תֹאכֵ֔לוּ לַכֶּ֖לֶב תַּשְׁלִכ֥וּן אֹתֽוֹ׃ס
records.gloss: And men of holiness you will be to me; and flesh in the field, torn, not you must eat; to the dog[s] you will throw it.
pieces: You shall be holy {{gender:people|men}} to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. Any meat torn by beasts out in the field is not for you to eat; it is to be thrown to the dogs.

L.30: And {{gender:people|men}} of holiness you shall be to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; and flesh torn [by beasts] in the field you shall not eat; to the dogs you shall throw it.

R.30: You belong to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you must be holy. When an animal is killed by wild animals out in the fields, its meat is not for you. Give it to the dogs.

decisions.choice: holy people to me: a people set apart for God
decisions.reason: God had called Israel to be "a holy nation" (19:6). Holiness reaches even to what they eat.

decisions.choice: flesh torn in the field: meat from an animal killed by a wild beast
decisions.reason: Such meat was unclean: the blood had not been drained and the animal had not been slaughtered properly (Leviticus 17:15; 22:8). It was not eaten but thrown to the dogs.

decisions.choice: You belong to me, and you must be holy
decisions.reason: Readable puts "to me" first, as belonging, and then the call to be holy.
